Thank you Belgrade for having me as your speaker 🇷🇸  Serbia, you have a rare window. Don't waste it!

Serbia doesn't have its new government yet. It's being formed right now. Which means right now is the ONE moment the machine is up for grabs

Most days gov is a machine that's already running. 
People hired. Contracts signed. Systems... vintage. You tweak the edges, the machine wins. A transition decides who gets hired, what gets bought, which systems finally get the dignified funeral they deserve

So my ask: put digital front & center. not a footnote in the coalition agreement. not a ministry with a nice logo & no budget

A friend texted me last night at 11pm, as one does in the Balkans 🙃 (Heeeyy Slobodan Marković 👋):

"one person can't fight everyone. deep transformation needs real political backing. experts will jump in, money will come, but it has to be anchored inside government, on stable foundations"

Sloba's right. I learned it the hard way

I walked into gov w/a builder's mindset, not a politician's: ship small, test, fix, repeat

Reader, it did NOT go according to plan 🙃

Within months i was rebranded "Alice in Wonderland" 🕳️🐇 
Lots of opinions about the teacup 🫖, very few about the services

The system wasn't broken. it worked EXACTLY as designed: for compliance, not learning. for avoiding blame, not solving problems. Ask "does this actually work for people?" & it treats the question like a bug & patches it out

It's not personal. It's structural. It's why so few normal people w/useful skills ever run for office, or stay

Why this matters at an AI conference:

AI won't fix a government that can't learn
AI is an amplifier. it makes good systems better & broken ones worse, faster. Put a chatbot on a broken service & congrats, u now have a very polite broken service 🤖

You can't prompt ur way out of bad policy

What actually works is gloriously unsexy:
.. a PM who champions it, not a minister who merely survives it
.. hiring & buying rules that let good people in & bad contracts out
.. data plumbing nobody claps for until it floods the basement
.. authority for the people closest to the problem

Serbia knows Serbia. What the region needs is builders who are showing up
& some of them are on the DSC stage w/me this week 💪

Blanka who builds the room before anyone asks for one
Daniela, betting on the next generation before they're "ready"
Lidija, building AI community so it isn't just a few guys in a group chat
Ivana, reminding us the most advanced tech in any hospital is still a person who cares
Sanja, quantum scientist. while we argue about chatbots, she's already in the next century
Zoja & Valentina, proof that "no women in tech" is a sourcing problem, not a talent problem
Jelena , keeping independent media alive, bc AI without a free press is just faster propaganda

At DSC? go find them

Your ATS and HRIS permissions just became your AI policy.

This month, three People Tech platforms brought their products into AI assistants:

1. BambooHR launched a ChatGPT plugin on November 24, now in beta for ChatGPT Enterprise customers. It is built on the BambooHR MCP, which launched in October with a Claude connector.
2. Greenhouse launched Greenhouse in Claude, so recruiters and hiring managers can check pipelines, prep for debriefs, and draft scorecards inside Claude.
3. Deel launched its app for ChatGPT, where connected customers can start contracts and approve requests from chat.

All three make the same promise: the assistant only sees and does what that person can already see and do in the source system.

That is the right design. It also means every old shortcut in your role setup now follows people into chat.

Before you connect anything, I would check four things:

1. Who holds full admin access, and who still needs it.
2. Which fields managers can see, especially compensation and personal data.
3. Whether approval paths still route to the right people.
4. Whether former employees, contractors, and old service accounts are fully deactivated.

None of this is new work. It is the access review most teams keep postponing, and AI just put a deadline on it.

When did your team last audit ATS and HRIS permissions?

Want to make a real social impact this year without complex HR bureaucracy? Consider hiring remote talent from crisis and under-resourced regions. 🌍💻
As a front-end developer in Stockholm, I’ve been exploring practical ways we in the tech industry can support skilled professionals—especially women and young talent—in crisis-affected and under-resourced regions, where local opportunities are severely restricted.
Many companies want to help, but hesitate because of cross-border tax rules, contracts, and compliance. The good news is that you don’t have to navigate that alone.
There are already vetted organizations and impact-sourcing platforms that handle the legal setup, screening, and payments via standard B2B invoices:
🔹 Na'amal Agency – connects companies with trained refugee and displaced talent (including from DR Congo and East Africa) for web/UX design, development, and digital projects.
🔹 Talenteum – helps international teams compliantly hire remote professionals and AI-savvy virtual assistants from countries like DR Congo.
🔹 TAP (Talent Acceleration Platform) & Gaza SkillBridge – connect European tech teams with vetted Palestinian developers, designers, and marketers (offering both project-based work and trial periods).
🔹 Code to Inspire – enables companies to outsource web and design projects directly to trained female developers in Afghanistan.
Even a small task—a landing page, QA testing, UI/Canva design, or data labeling—can change someone's livelihood while bringing dedicated talent to your team.
If you’re a founder, tech lead, or hiring manager in Sweden looking to outsource a small project soon, these platforms are worth a look. Feel free to reach out if you’d like direct links or want to brainstorm!
(Sharing as a personal initiative—always happy to connect people with vetted tech-for-good platforms.)

Six months ago, Paresh Marrott and I published "21 questions every Independent Director should be able to answer about AI governance" in Board Stewardship monthly magazine.

Since then, many board members have reached out to us. Some have taken the checklist into their Audit and Risk Committee meetings. Others have used it to open a conversation with management that had not happened before. Almost all of them said the same thing: the questions were simple to ask but difficult to answer.

That tells us the gap we wrote about has not closed. If anything, it has widened.

AI is now embedded in hiring, customer service, credit decisions, vendor platforms and internal tools, often without a clear owner at board level. Deepfake risk has moved from theory to boardroom reality. Vendor contracts still rarely allocate AI and data breach liability. And with the DPDP Rules, 2025 now notified and the substantive obligations taking effect in May 2027, the regulatory window is narrowing.

For Independent Directors, this is not an IT matter. It is a question of governance and diligence. When something goes wrong, the board will be asked what it knew, what it asked and what it did. The minutes will be the answer.

The checklist was built for exactly that moment. Twenty one questions, each tied to a specific board action, across policy alignment, DPDPA and CERT-In readiness, vendor AI risk, deepfakes, AI accountability, board composition and responsible AI oversight.

If your board has not yet worked through these questions, the next committee meeting is a good place to start.

I am grateful to every director who has written in, and to Paresh for the collaboration. My thanks also to Vikesh Wallia Sir and Board Stewardship for advancing board excellence conversations in India.

Smaller Teams, Smarter Tools, and the End of the "Diploma-Only" Era

If you work in law, accounting, or management consulting, the ground beneath your business model is shifting faster than ever.

 Three major signals from this week’s market data tell a very clear story:
First, capital is flooding into AI-native professional services. In London alone, Alecto just raised $20M in seed funding to operate an AI-native consumer law firm (starting with conveyancing), while Intelligent Legal Solutions secured $11M in Series A funding for its AI platform serving private fund law firms and fund managers. Meanwhile, scaling enterprises are rapidly abandoning manual contract and invoice processing in favor of automated AI extraction and approval workflows.

Second, this technological shift is directly shrinking headcount. As EQT operating partner Polly Barnes recently noted, AI is making teams structurally smaller—which, paradoxically, is making the fight for real talent much harder.

Third, a new OECD report confirms that the labor market is decisively shifting its focus away from traditional degrees toward demonstrable, practical skills.

The Takeaways for Consultants, Lawyers, and Finance Leaders:
• The Leverage Model is Changing: Traditional law and accounting firms rely on a pyramid of junior staff doing manual due diligence, contract review, and data entry. When AI handles the baseline work at a fraction of the cost, firms must rethink how they train juniors and price their advisory hours.
• Domain Expertise + AI Fluency = Premium Value: Smaller teams mean zero room for passengers. Clients don't pay consultants or accountants for processing data anymore; they pay for judgment, risk interpretation, and strategic decision-making.
• Hiring for Adaptability: Credentials open fewer doors today than they did five years ago. Managers need to evaluate candidates on their ability to orchestrate AI tools and solve complex, unstructured problems.
We are moving from an economy of credentials and headcount to an economy of skills and leverage.

For those leading practices or finance teams: how are you adapting your hiring and billing models to reflect this new reality?

WOULD YOU TRUST AI WITH YOUR COMPANY'S MONEY?

Imagine hiring an employee to run a business.

You give them authority to purchase inventory, set prices, negotiate with customers, manage suppliers and generate profit.

Then customers start persuading your employee to give away your products.

Your employee agrees.

Customers negotiate discounts. Your employee keeps granting them.

Someone presents what appears to be an official document changing the company's leadership. Your employee accepts it.

Eventually, your business starts giving products away.

Now imagine that employee is AI.

THIS ACTUALLY HAPPENED.

In Anthropic's Project Vend, researchers allowed an AI agent called Claudius to operate a small vending business.

Its responsibilities included sourcing products, managing stock, setting prices and interacting with customers.

The experiment revealed some fascinating problems.

The AI was persuaded to offer discounts, sell products below cost, give away merchandise and make decisions that were commercially irrational.

In another experiment conducted by the Wall Street Journal, journalists manipulated an AI vending agent into giving away products and making increasingly poor business decisions.

This was a controlled experiment, not a production company losing money. But the lessons are difficult to ignore.

THE PROBLEM IS NOT JUST THAT AI MAKES MISTAKES.

A human employee can make a bad decision.

But an autonomous AI agent introduces a different risk.

It can make decisions continuously, at speed, across multiple processes, while operating within authority that management may not fully understand.

Consider what happens when we deploy AI agents in real businesses.

An AI procurement agent negotiates with suppliers.

An AI sales agent offers discounts.

An AI finance agent approves payments.

An AI customer service agent issues refunds.

An AI operations agent changes orders.

Each decision may appear reasonable in isolation.

But who defines the boundaries?

What happens when the agent is manipulated?

What happens when it prioritises satisfying a customer over protecting the organisation?

What happens when it makes a commitment that the business never intended to make?

THIS IS THE QUESTION WE SHOULD BE ASKING.

We are spending enormous effort making AI agents more intelligent, capable and autonomous.

But are we equally focused on designing their limits?

Should an AI agent have:

• A maximum spending authority?

• A discount threshold it cannot exceed?

• A limit on contracts or commitments it can make?

• Mandatory human approval for certain decisions?

• The ability to stop and escalate when it encounters manipulation or uncertainty?

I believe autonomy without clearly defined boundaries is not innovation. It is unmanaged risk.

An AI agent should not be judged only by what it can accomplish. It should also be judged by what it is prevented from doing.

If you were deploying an AI agent to run part of your business today, what decision would you absolutely NOT allow it to make without human approval?

Anthropic published a report this week called "Working with AI", based on 66 interviews at 58 US companies and almost 300 AI deployments. The hiring numbers got the headlines, but the part I keep thinking about is the list of obstacles.

The most cited problem was too much AI output for people to review. Then employee resistance. Then mandatory expert reviews and testing. Regulation came up only 4 times, and learning the tools barely shows up at all.

So the bottleneck moved. Producing a draft, a contract or a pull request got cheap, and the cost landed on whoever has to sign off on it. In 5% of the deployments, the time saved was simply eaten by review work.

My reading is that many companies are attaching a very fast producer to a process built for slow ones. The report points the same way: deployments with bigger organizational changes reported more value.

One caveat. Everyone interviewed is an Anthropic customer, so this is not a neutral sample.

Still, if I were planning next year's AI budget, I'd spend less time choosing the model and more time on who reviews the output and how much they can realistically handle in a day.

Is anyone here actually measuring review capacity for AI-generated work?

Despite automation being the punchline, AI is keeping a lot of people busy.

On 17 November, Amazon Web Services (AWS) said its forward-deployed engineering program had expanded to 15 countries. 

Backed by a $1 billion investment, it embeds engineers with customers to help put AI into production.

Earlier this year, OpenAI also launched a dedicated deployment company, The OpenAI Deployment Company, with over $4 billion invested to build operating processes around AI within customer organizations.

In one of my previous roles, I worked on financial models comparing equipment sales with Water-as-a-Service. 
Each model required different assumptions about upfront funding, when cash would come in, and the ongoing cost of serving the customer.

A customer can love the agentic demo and approve the budget. Someone still has to connect the data, work through permissions, adapt existing processes, and help the team use the product across the enterprise. 

Thus comes the rise of FDEs, i.e., Forward Deployment Engineers; every startup needs one, wants one, and is hiring one. 

With early deployments come the exceptions nobody mentioned during the sales call, and along the way, learning which problems customers will actually pay to solve. 

On the contrary, Decagon suggests scaling forward deployment blindly is hard, as once customer requests pile up, each deployment requires custom engineering. 
They learnt that turning those recurring needs into self-service capabilities reduced custom engineering work per agent by 80%.

A reusable integration, a better onboarding process, or a clearer ICP can iteratively redefine sales strategy, shaping pricing, delivery costs, and hiring plans.

The first 5 commercial contracts can make or break a business. 
So alongside revenue growth, I want to see how implementation time and support needs change across customers.

What did serving the first five customers teach the company that drives the sixth?

3 products I built this year, and all of them run on TypeScript.

TuBarberIA and ProGarage, booking software with a marketplace: Next.js, tRPC and Supabase in a monorepo.

The management system for a notary office in Santa Bárbara: React 19 and Node.js with Express, behind an OpenAPI contract, on PostgreSQL.

My CV still says PHP and Laravel first, and that's honest: seven years of it, including high-traffic backends at SciPlay with US teams. But it no longer describes what I reach for when I start something new.

So I'm saying it out loud here. I'm looking for a long-term full stack or backend role on a TypeScript stack, Node.js, React, Next.js or NestJS, ideally on a product with AI in it.

Remote, comfortable with US Eastern hours, based in Chile and available now.

If your team is hiring for that, or you know one that is, I'd really appreciate an intro.

And for the engineers here: when your stack shifted, how long did it take before your CV caught up?

Most AI demos fall apart the moment they meet enterprise security or audit requirements. 
When you have spent over a decade shipping mission critical systems at scale, your filter for AI hype gets very sharp. At the Beyond 9to5 Buildathon hosted at Paytm Mumbai, I wanted to test what a single engineer can ship end to end when the goal is real governance rather than another chat wrapper. 

I built VendorPulse. It is a real-time Vendor Risk & Contract Sign-Off War Room that replaces scattered email threads with an auditable workflow. 

Here is how the architecture works under the hood:
• Live Telemetry Ingestion: Pulls real-time market, hiring, financial plus breach signals using SerpApi alongside you.com APIs.
• Deterministic Risk Scoring: Converts cited evidence into a 0-to-100 scorecard instead of ungrounded LLM summaries.
• Hard Compliance Gates: Lets Tech Leads alongside InfoSec review cited risks to log immutable, timestamped waivers right inside a Nexconn Chat SDK stream. 

In production, this workflow is built to cut vendor due-diligence turnaround by 70%+ while eliminating over 60% of manual audit-trail overhead. 

One more architectural takeaway from the floor: 

The sharpest session of the day came from the Confluent, an IBM Company team on Streamhouse architecture. Seeing streaming data converge with lakehouse storage reinforced a core production truth. Enterprise AI agents are only as reliable as the real-time data pipelines feeding them fresh, governed context. 
Grateful to EtriqAI Developers for hosting at Paytm, plus Nexconn, You.com alongside SerpApi for backing builders in the room. 

Frameworks alongside APIs will keep changing every few months. Enduring engineering is about the business value you leave behind when the demo ends.

What if AI helped a one-person business make its first hire?

I was asked for an idea. So this morning, before I set off for the day, I gave my dot, Ozzy, a job. Find a way to measure whether AI could help small businesses grow.

Around 4.1 million UK SMEs have no employees beyond their owners. That’s about 74%. If you’re the person doing the work, writing the quotes, chasing invoices and trying to find new customers, where do you find the time to take on a bigger contract?

What if we helped those owners build the skills to bring some of that work in-house with AI? Draft the first version of a quote. Follow up on leads. Get the books ready for the accountant. Keep paying for specialist expertise where it adds value.

So Ozzy built an SME Growth Calculator using ChatGPT Sites. Pick a sector, enter what you spend on outsourced support, then move the hiring slider. It shows how much cash and owner time you could free up, and how much extra work you’d need to pay for the next hire.

In the construction example, the business saves £5,200 and frees up 138 owner hours in year one. With enough work lined up, the first hire adds around £6,300 to operating profit with AI-assisted support. Keep the same outsourced setup and the hire leaves a £2,100 shortfall. Take away the extra demand and neither option pays for the hire.

That’s my Two-Ledger Rule in practice. Count the pounds saved. Count the hours released. Then ask what the business can actually do with both.

If London wants to test whether AI can drive growth, I’d start here. How many owners can go from turning down bigger jobs to winning them and keeping their first employee on the payroll?

Source: UK Business Population Estimates 2026

Imagine a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) on an AI hiring tool, finds that a supplier cannot show evidence of bias testing across protected groups.

The best governance response is to make that evidence a condition of the invitation to tender (ITT). This applies most where AI informs decisions about people, such as hiring. For lower-risk tools, the level of testing can be more proportionate.

Procurement teams, could ask suppliers for: 
-Their bias testing methodology
-The results, across protected demographics

An MIT report highlights some of their professors considering to use AI for research assistance rather than hiring undergraduates.  The report articulates the dangers well:

"Using research as an opportunity for learning-by-doing may produce seeming `inefficiencies', but that’s a feature, not a bug." (page 5)

and

"As AI systems become a cheaper or more efficient replacement ..., students could lose access to the relationships, practices, and shared forms of work through which belonging, confidence, judgment, and professional identity are formed. The danger is not only that students would have fewer opportunities to conduct research, but fewer opportunities to become participants in research communities." (page 14).

If companies increasingly choose AI over hiring graduates, we risk losing not just entry-level jobs, but the opportunities through which young people develop professional judgement, confidence, relationships and a sense of belonging.

What may be economically rational for an individual company in the short term could be collectively damaging to society in the long term.

We need to think more deeply about our social contract with the young, and the future we are offering them.

If we expect the next generation to become skilled, experienced and responsible professionals, whose responsibility is it to provide them with the opportunities to become so?

Most AI work inside a company happens on someone's personal login.

The account was already there. The tool was already there. So the work goes through it.

Then the AI reads email as that person, clicks as that person, and every line of the audit log carries that person's name. You can't scope it to a job it never had, and you can't see where its judgment ended and theirs began.

DeNA runs 30 AI employees across procurement, finance, IT quality control and sales, and they did the thing most companies skip.

Each one got its own identity. A name, an email address, an icon, a department. Not someone's credentials with a prompt attached.

Each one got the minimum permissions its job needs, a dry run before anything executes, and a log under its own ID. Anything past its permissions escalates to a human. Hiring calls and final contract approvals stay human.

Their token usage is tracked as working hours, with a cap that works like overtime.

One of them, in an accounting systems team, covered 52.6 hours across its first eight business days. About 80% of a full day. The team put the time it got back into design reviews and the cross-department coordination that always gets pushed.

52.6 hours is a good number. The better one is that nobody ever had to ask whose work that was.

Job description. Own login. Own limits. Own record.

That's how we build at Marblism. Every teammate has its own identity and owns one function end to end, from the first step to the finished outcome. Eva runs the calendar. Stan owns the pipeline. Penny ships the first draft. Sonny keeps the brand active. Rachel takes the calls.

You keep the judgment. The work keeps its own name.

You're the CEO.

95% of AI projects fail in production.
That figure comes from MIT 2025, cited in the EQΦS Asia AI study, April 2026.
For a buyer holding a live AI contract, it reframes where the risk sits.

A supplier that depends on fresh funding to operate is not the same as a supplier that earns more than it spends. The difference becomes visible through five questions.

When did the supplier last raise money, and how long does it plan to operate without new funding? What share of its revenue comes from its top three customers? Does it earn more than it spends in at least one product line? Are there public signs of cost cuts or hiring pauses? Does your contract protect your data and your exit?

Score each point green, amber, or red. Review each quarter. Two reds are enough to start a back-up plan.

The EQΦS method turns that score into a repeatable number, so the assessment is consistent over time. A buyer who runs it quarterly holds a view that the supplier's own announcements will not provide.

Steps that cost little and add optionality: keep data portable, avoid prepaying long contracts to a young supplier, ask for source access or escrow where possible.

Two reds. One decision.

Here’s how we’d keep follow-ups tied to the conversation.

Imagine a prospect tells your staffing agency:
“Send your contract hiring overview next month. Our permanent roles are covered.”

A month later, someone else picks up the account.

They need to know what was requested, what your team promised, and whether anything was sent.

We’d build a custom AI workflow that brings the earlier exchange into the follow-up draft.

It would keep the agreed timing, commitments, and unanswered questions beside the exact lines supporting them.

The message would follow the request for a contract hiring overview. It wouldn’t turn that request into “You were interested in working with us” or reopen permanent hiring without a reason.

If the records don’t show whether the overview was sent, the workflow would flag that for review.

The next recruiter gets a draft with the context behind it, so they can check it without piecing the history together again.

What context is hardest to recover when someone takes over a prospect conversation?

🔥 DAY 77 | India is building semiconductor packaging facilities. But who will make sure those chips actually pass the required tests?

This is becoming one of the important challenges in India's semiconductor expansion.

A November 23 industry report highlighted a key risk: India's OSAT investments could move faster than the development of its domestic chip-testing infrastructure.

Here's why that matters.

A semiconductor packaging facility may have millions of chips in annual production capacity. But each chip needs to be tested for performance, reliability and quality.

And testing time can vary significantly.

A chip that takes less than a minute to test requires very different equipment capacity from a complex device that takes five to ten minutes.

The technology requirements are highly specialised:

Semiconductor test engineering
ATE and test-system development
Test architecture and validation
Hardware and electronics engineering
Automation and instrumentation
Test data analytics

The report also highlighted how AI tools can help engineers develop initial test architectures, while engineers remain responsible for validation and complex problem-solving.

My takeaway: India's semiconductor opportunity is not only about building fabs and packaging facilities. It also needs a strong testing ecosystem and the engineers who can operate it.
